items.name: Sign in with email and password
items.description: The system allows an employee to authenticate using an email address and a password through the sign-in screen (S-01) and the public POST /api/auth/login endpoint. Both fields are required; when either is missing or invalid the request is rejected with field-level validation feedback. On success the backend issues a signed, expiring token that represents the session, the My incidents screen opens, and the token is stored securely on the device. On failure the application displays a single generic message that does not reveal whether the email exists. The sign-in button remains disabled while the request is processing to prevent duplicate submissions.
items.business_value: Secure authentication is the entry point to every protected capability, ensuring that each employee only reaches their own incident data.
preconditions: The user account exists and is active
The backend is reachable over the network
postconditions: A valid signed session token is issued and stored on the device
The employee can access their own incidents
business_rules: Both email and password are required
Failed authentication shows a generic message that does not reveal whether the email exists
The sign-in button stays disabled while the request is processing
acceptance_criteria: Given an active employee with a valid password, when the employee signs in, then the My incidents screen opens and the password does not appear in logs or responses.
Given invalid credentials, when sign-in is attempted, then a generic message is displayed and the system does not reveal whether the email exists.

items.name: Sign out
items.description: An authenticated employee can sign out from the My incidents screen (S-02 includes the Sign out action). When the user signs out, the locally stored session token is deleted from the device so that no protected screen remains accessible. Any subsequent navigation to a protected screen requires a new sign-in. This closes the session lifecycle started at sign-in and prevents token reuse on a shared or lost device.
items.business_value: Allows employees to end their session cleanly, protecting incident data on shared or lost devices.
preconditions: The user is authenticated and holds a locally stored token
postconditions: Protected screens are no longer accessible without signing in again
business_rules: Signing out deletes the locally stored token
acceptance_criteria: Given an authenticated user, when the user signs out, then the local token is removed and protected screens are no longer accessible.

items.name: View my incidents list
items.description: After authentication the employee lands on the My incidents screen (S-02), which displays only the incidents owned by the authenticated employee, fetched through GET /api/incidents. Each list item shows the title, category, priority, status, and creation date. The default order is newest first by creation date. The screen must cover loading, empty, error, and content states, with a retry path when a network error occurs, and it exposes a visible action to create a new incident plus the Sign out action. Employees cannot view incidents owned by other users.
items.business_value: Gives employees a clear, private overview of their reported issues so they can track what is open and what is resolved.
preconditions: The user is authenticated with a valid token
postconditions: Only incidents owned by the authenticated employee are displayed
The list is ordered from newest to oldest
business_rules: Display only incidents owned by the authenticated employee
Default order: newest first
Each item shows title, category, priority, status, and creation date
acceptance_criteria: Given an authenticated employee, when the list loads, then only incidents owned by that employee are shown, ordered newest first.
Given slow, empty, or failed responses, when the incident list opens, then the interface respectively displays loading, empty, or recoverable error states.

items.name: Filter incidents by status
items.description: The My incidents screen provides a status filter with the options All, Pending, In progress, and Resolved. When the employee selects a filter, the application requests or narrows the incident list so that only incidents whose status matches the selection are displayed; All removes the restriction. Statuses are the fixed set Pending, In progress, and Resolved. Filtering applies on top of owner isolation, so a filter never exposes another employee's incidents.
items.business_value: Lets employees quickly focus on the incidents that matter, for example everything still pending.
postconditions: Only incidents matching the selected status are displayed
business_rules: Available statuses: Pending, In progress, Resolved
Filter options: All, Pending, In progress, Resolved
acceptance_criteria: Given incidents in multiple statuses, when a status filter is selected, then only matching incidents are displayed.

items.name: Create a new incident
items.description: From the My incidents screen the employee opens the New incident form (S-03) and submits it via POST /api/incidents. The form requires a title of 5 to 100 characters, a description of 10 to 1,000 characters, one category (Systems, Equipment, Access, or Other) and one priority (Low, Medium, or High). Validation is enforced on both client and server, and errors appear next to the corresponding fields. Every new incident is created in Pending status, owned by the authenticated employee. Duplicate submissions are prevented while the request is processing, and after a successful save the app returns to the list and shows a confirmation.
items.business_value: Enables employees to report issues about systems, equipment, and access so support can track and resolve them.
postconditions: Exactly one Pending incident owned by the authenticated employee is created
The employee returns to the list with a confirmation and sees the new incident
business_rules: Title required, 5-100 characters
Description required, 10-1000 characters
Category required: Systems, Equipment, Access, Other
Priority required: Low, Medium, High
Every new incident starts in Pending status
Prevent duplicate submissions while the request is processing
acceptance_criteria: Given a valid form, when it is saved, then exactly one Pending incident is created and appears in the list.
Given an invalid form, when Save is selected, then the incident is not successfully created and validation errors appear next to the relevant fields.

items.name: View incident details and status history
items.description: From the incident list the employee opens the Incident details screen (S-04), served by GET /api/incidents/{id} for the owner. The screen shows the identifier, title, description, category, priority, status as a text badge, and creation date, followed by a simple chronological status-history timeline built from IncidentHistory entries. Employees cannot edit the owner or alter the history. When the incident does not exist or is owned by another employee, the API and the app return a safe result that does not leak information about other users' incidents. The screen includes navigation back to the incident list.
items.business_value: Lets employees follow the progress of their reported issues and understand what happened at each status change.
preconditions: The incident is owned by the requesting employee (otherwise a safe response is returned)
postconditions: Incident data and its chronological history are displayed for the owner
Non-owner or missing-incident requests receive a safe response without information disclosure
business_rules: Employees cannot edit the owner or alter history
Requests for a missing or foreign incident must return a safe result without leaking information
acceptance_criteria: Given an authenticated employee, when the employee requests an incident owned by another user, then the API returns a safe response without exposing the other user's data.
Given an owned incident, when details open, then the primary data and the chronological status history are displayed.

items.name: Support agent updates incident status
items.description: A support agent updates an incident's status through the PATCH /api/incidents/{id}/status endpoint, which is protected by role so that only the support role can call it; an employee who attempts it receives a forbidden response. Valid transitions follow the linear path Pending to In progress to Resolved, and a Resolved incident cannot return to a previous status in version 1. Every accepted status change records a history entry with the previous status, new status, date, and actor, and this history is immutable for employees. This version does not require a support mobile screen; the capability is API-only and must be covered by API tests.
items.business_value: Allows the support team to drive incidents to resolution while keeping a trustworthy, tamper-proof progress trail for employees.
preconditions: The actor holds the support role
postconditions: The incident status is updated when the transition is valid
An immutable history entry records the transition
business_rules: Only the support role can update incident status
Valid transitions are Pending to In progress to Resolved
A Resolved incident cannot return to a previous status in version 1
Each transition records previous status, new status, date, and actor
acceptance_criteria: Given an authorized update, when support changes incident status, then an immutable history entry is recorded.
Given a normal employee, when the employee attempts to update status through the API, then the API returns a forbidden response.
source_refs: Page 4 (FR-009, FR-010; Section 6 BR-004 to BR-007)

items.name: API health check
items.description: The API exposes a public GET /health endpoint used for operational validation of the service. It reports that the API is up and able to respond, without requiring authentication and without disclosing sensitive configuration, stack traces, or internal details. Deployment and local-run tooling use it to verify that the backend started correctly before the Android client is exercised against it.
items.business_value: Provides a simple operational probe so teams and scripts can confirm the backend is running before use.
postconditions: The endpoint reports service health without leaking sensitive information
business_rules: Health responses must not expose stack traces or sensitive information
acceptance_criteria: Given a running backend, when GET /health is called, then the service reports healthy without requiring authentication.

items.name: Development demo data seed
items.description: Development initialization creates a small, consistent set of demo records: one employee (empleado@minisoporte.test), one support agent whose email is supplied through configuration, and three employee incidents covering one Pending, one In progress, and one Resolved status, including consistent history entries for the incidents whose status has changed. Passwords are read exclusively from the DEMO_EMPLOYEE_PASSWORD and DEMO_SUPPORT_PASSWORD environment variables; if either value is missing the seed fails with a clear message and no default password is embedded in source code. The seed is idempotent and never creates demo accounts automatically in production environments.
items.business_value: Gives testers and reviewers a ready, realistic dataset for internal validation without weakening production security.
preconditions: The environment is development or demonstration
postconditions: Demo employee, support agent, and three incidents exist with consistent history
The seed can be re-run without duplicating records
business_rules: Demo passwords come only from DEMO_EMPLOYEE_PASSWORD and DEMO_SUPPORT_PASSWORD
Missing password variables fail the seed with a clear message
No default password may be embedded in source code
Seed is idempotent and never runs automatically in production
acceptance_criteria: Given a development environment with both password variables set, when the seed runs, then the demo employee, support agent, and three incidents with consistent history are created.
Given either password variable is missing, when the seed runs, then initialization fails with a clear message and no default password is used.

items.name: Incident owner isolation
items.description: An incident belongs to exactly one employee, and the system must enforce owner-based authorization on every incident query: an employee cannot view incidents owned by another employee. This rule applies to the list, the detail endpoint, and any history data, including missing or foreign identifiers, which must produce a safe response that does not leak information. Violation would expose private incident data across users, breaking the core confidentiality promise of the product and failing acceptance criteria AC-03.
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Enforce owner authorization on every incident query)

items.name: Initial incident status is Pending
items.description: Every incident created by an employee starts its lifecycle in the Pending status; no other initial status is permitted. The creation flow and the database defaults must both enforce this so a client cannot submit an incident directly as In progress or Resolved. Violation would corrupt the status lifecycle, mislead support triage, and break the status-history model, which records the initial creation with an optional empty previous status.

items.name: Linear status transitions with Resolved as terminal
items.description: The only valid status transitions are Pending to In progress and In progress to Resolved, and a Resolved incident cannot return to a previous status in version 1. The status-update endpoint must validate transitions before applying them and reject any backwards, skipped, or repeated transition. This keeps the incident lifecycle meaningful for employees reviewing history; a violation would allow misleading progress records such as a resolved issue silently reopening without a trail.

items.name: Only the support role can update incident status
items.description: Updating an incident's status is reserved for users with the support role; employees can create and read their own incidents but never change status. The PATCH /api/incidents/{id}/status endpoint must be protected by role and covered by API tests proving an ordinary employee receives a forbidden response. Without this rule the owner-based separation of duties collapses, since reporters could mark their own issues as resolved.
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Protect the status-update endpoint by role)

items.name: Every status change records an immutable history entry
items.description: Each accepted status transition must create an IncidentHistory entry capturing the previous status, the new status, the date, and the actor who made the change; the initial creation may leave previous_status empty. Employees cannot edit the owner or alter the history, making the timeline a trustworthy audit trail. Violation would leave status changes unexplained, undermine employee trust, and fail acceptance criterion AC-07.

items.name: Email normalization and uniqueness
items.description: Email addresses are normalized (trimmed and lowercased) before authentication and must be unique in the User table. The uniqueness constraint prevents duplicate accounts from being confused at sign-in, while normalization ensures the same address typed in different cases still matches one account. Violation would allow ambiguous identities or failed sign-ins for legitimate users.
source_refs: Page 5 (Section 8 User email unique and normalized)

items.name: Generic authentication failure messages
items.description: When authentication fails, the application displays one generic message that does not reveal whether the email exists in the system. This prevents user-enumeration attacks in which an attacker probes valid email addresses by observing different errors for unknown users versus wrong passwords. Violation would leak account existence and facilitate targeted attacks against employees.

items.name: Passwords stored only as salted hashes and never logged
items.description: Passwords must never be logged or stored as plain text; the backend stores only resistant salted hashes in the password_hash field, and passwords never appear in API responses or logs. This limits the impact of any database or log exposure, since attackers would face salted hashes rather than reusable credentials. Violation would directly compromise employee accounts and breach the project's security standards (OWASP Top 10 / OWASP Mobile).
source_refs: Page 3 (Section 4.1 Passwords must never be logged or stored as plain text)
Page 6 (Section 10 Store passwords only as resistant salted hashes)

items.name: No sensitive data in logs or error responses
items.description: Technical logs must not contain passwords, tokens, authorization headers, or other sensitive personal data, and API errors must use a consistent response format without stack traces or sensitive information. This applies to every endpoint, including the health check, and to the Android application's own logging. Violation would expose credentials and internal details to anyone with log access and would leak information useful for attacks.
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 9 Errors; Section 10 Never log passwords, tokens, or authorization headers)
Page 7 (Section 11 Technical logs must not contain sensitive personal data)

items.name: Demo seed restricted to non-production and driven by environment secrets
items.description: Initial demo records are created only in development or demonstration environments, and never automatically in production. Seed passwords come solely from the DEMO_EMPLOYEE_PASSWORD and DEMO_SUPPORT_PASSWORD environment variables; a missing variable must fail the seed with a clear message, and no default password may be embedded in source code. The seed must be idempotent. Violation would either place hardcoded credentials into the codebase or create live demo accounts in production.

items.name: Validate data on both client and server with field-level errors
items.description: All form data must be validated on both the Android client and the REST backend; when validation fails on the New incident screen, the incident is not created and errors appear next to the corresponding fields. Server-side validation is the authoritative guard against malformed or malicious requests, while client-side validation gives immediate feedback. Violation would allow invalid incidents into the database or leave users confused about why a save failed.
source_refs: Page 3 (Section 4.3; S-03 validation errors next to fields)
Page 6 (Section 10 Validate data on both client and server)

items.name: Accessibility and visual differentiation rules
items.description: The interface must provide readable labels, sufficient contrast, and appropriate touch targets, and statuses must be differentiated with both text and color, never color alone. The visual style is professional and restrained, using the defined palette (dark green #1E3A2A primary, yellow #EFC64E accent, light background #F5F7F5), 8-pixel corners, spacing in multiples of eight, compact list cards, and no side navigation since the app targets a phone. Violation would exclude users with visual impairments and produce ambiguous status recognition.

items.name: Mandatory tests with 90 percent coverage of business logic
items.description: The backend must include unit tests for business rules and integration tests for authorization (ownership isolation and role protection of the status endpoint), targeting 90 percent coverage of relevant business logic. These tests are the executable proof that BR rules and authorization constraints hold; without them, regressions in owner isolation or role enforcement could reach the internal-test build unnoticed. Violation fails the stated acceptance criteria and the project's quality threshold.
source_refs: Page 7 (Section 11 Unit and integration tests; 90 percent coverage)
Page 2 (Section 3 status endpoint covered by API tests)

items.name: Signed token sessions with expiration and role-based authorization
items.description: Authentication must use signed tokens with expiration and signature validation, and the backend must enforce role-based authorization (employee versus support) on protected endpoints. Successful authentication returns this token-based session, and a token is issued only for valid credentials. Without signed, expiring tokens the API would be open to forged or never-expiring sessions, undermining owner isolation and the role protection of the status endpoint.
items.technical_detail: Signed tokens with expiration and signature validation; token issued only for valid credentials; roles: employee, support
source_refs: Page 3 (Section 4.1 Successful authentication returns a token-based session)
Page 6 (Section 10 Use signed tokens with expiration and signature validation; Protect the status-update endpoint by role)
Page 6 (Section 12 Authentication requirement: signed token and role-based authorization)

items.name: Android Keystore-backed token storage
items.description: The Android application must store the session token using Android Keystore-backed storage, never as plain text. This protects the session token from extraction by other apps or from a compromised device filesystem, keeping the session valid only for the legitimate holder of the device. Without it, a plain-text token file would let any local attacker hijack the employee's session; signing out must delete this stored token.
items.technical_detail: Token stored via Android Keystore-backed storage; deleted on sign out; never plain text
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Store the mobile token using Android Keystore-backed storage, never as plain text)
Page 3 (Section 4.1 Signing out deletes the locally stored token)

items.name: Rate limiting on sign-in attempts
items.description: The sign-in endpoint must enforce rate limiting on failed authentication attempts to slow down brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks against employee accounts. The limiter applies to POST /api/auth/login and must not leak whether an email exists through different throttling behavior. Without it, attackers could try unlimited password guesses against known employee email addresses.
items.technical_detail: Rate limiting applied to POST /api/auth/login sign-in attempts

items.name: HTTPS required outside the local environment
items.description: All client-server communication outside the local development environment must use HTTPS so that credentials, tokens, and incident data are encrypted in transit. Local development may run plain HTTP for convenience, but the deployed internal-test setup must reject cleartext traffic. Without enforced HTTPS, tokens and passwords would be exposed to network interception.
items.technical_detail: HTTPS mandatory outside local environment; cleartext allowed only locally
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Require HTTPS outside the local environment)

items.name: Parameterized queries or ORM to prevent injection
items.description: All database access must use parameterized queries or an ORM so that user-supplied values (emails, titles, filters, identifiers) are never concatenated into SQL strings. This prevents SQL injection against the PostgreSQL database that stores users, incidents, and history. Without it, a crafted input field could read or modify any user's data, directly defeating owner isolation.
items.technical_detail: Parameterized queries or ORM for all database access; no string-concatenated SQL
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Use parameterized queries or an ORM to prevent injection)

items.name: Secrets supplied via environment variables and excluded from Git
items.description: All application secrets must be supplied through environment variables, and keystores, .env files, key.properties, and credentials must be excluded from source control. Release builds are prepared for externally supplied signing secrets without containing any real secrets, and a release build without signing variables must fail clearly rather than substitute a debug signing key. Violation would leak credentials into the repository and could produce an insecurely signed release APK.
items.technical_detail: Secrets via environment variables; Git excludes keystores, .env, key.properties, credentials; release build fails clearly without signing variables (AC-11)
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Supply secrets through environment variables; Exclude keystores, .env, key.properties, and credentials from Git)
Page 8-9 (AC-11; Section 17 Release configuration prepared for externally supplied signing secrets)

items.name: No Android permissions and no push notifications
items.description: The Android application must declare no Android permissions in this version and must not include push notifications, deep links, or offline operation. Only explicitly selected Android permissions may be enabled, and this version requires none, which minimizes the attack surface and simplifies the internal-test approval. Violation would add device capabilities the customer explicitly excluded and could fail the build review.
items.technical_detail: Android permissions: none; push notifications disabled; deep links out of scope; offline operation disabled
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 10 Enable only explicitly selected Android permissions, this version requires none; Section 12 Push notifications: disabled; Deep links: out of scope; Offline operation: disabled)
Page 2 (Section 1 does not include push notifications, offline operation)

items.name: Reproducible database migrations on PostgreSQL
items.description: The database layer must use reproducible migrations so that any environment can rebuild an identical schema from version control. The data model comprises User (UUID id, unique normalized email, password_hash, role, active, created_at), Incident (UUID id, owner_id reference to User, title, description, category, priority, status, created_at, updated_at), and IncidentHistory (UUID id, incident_id, optional previous_status, new_status, changed_by, changed_at). Per the Target system selections the engine is PostgreSQL 16.15 with foreign keys, constraints, and indexes. Without reproducible migrations, environments would drift and seeds or tests would fail unpredictably.
items.technical_detail: PostgreSQL 16.15; tables User, Incident, IncidentHistory with UUID ids, foreign keys (owner_id, incident_id, changed_by), unique email, status values pending/in_progress/resolved, category systems/equipment/access/other, priority low/medium/high
source_refs: Page 7 (Section 11 Database migrations must be reproducible)
Page 6 (Section 12 database engine selected in Target system)

items.name: Android phone in portrait, Spanish UI, online only
items.description: The mobile client targets Android phones in portrait orientation only, with the user interface language in Spanish, and operates online only; no offline synchronization is required or provided. Network errors must not crash the application and must always provide a retry path, and the target API response time is under two seconds under normal conditions. Violation would break the declared form factor, confuse Spanish-speaking employees, or produce a fragile app on flaky networks.
items.technical_detail: Form factor: phone portrait; UI language: Spanish; online only; no crash on network errors with retry; API response under 2 seconds
source_refs: Page 9 (Section 15 Do not use side navigation; designed for a phone)

items.name: Internal-testing Android build and run.apps contract
items.description: The project must deliver an installable debug APK for internal validation built from the selected mobile toolchain (Kotlin/Jetpack Compose, application id com.nexti.minisoporte), plus a run.apps contract containing a build-only mobile application and an HTTP backend, and a release configuration prepared for externally supplied signing secrets without real ones. Running the declared tests, lint checks, and Android build command must produce the APK without requiring production secrets. Distribution is internal testing only; Google Play publication is out of scope. Without this packaging the reviewers cannot install or run the product.
items.technical_detail: Internal distribution; debug APK; run.apps contract (build-only mobile app + HTTP backend); release config for external signing secrets; application id com.nexti.minisoporte; Kotlin Android
source_refs: Page 8-9 (AC-10; Section 17 Expected deliverables; Debug APK for internal validation)

items.name: REST API surface built on FastAPI
items.description: The backend exposes the proposed REST surface: public POST /api/auth/login to authenticate, authenticated GET /api/me to return the current user, employee-accessible GET /api/incidents (list with optional status filter) and POST /api/incidents (create), owner-restricted GET /api/incidents/{id} (details and history), support-only PATCH /api/incidents/{id}/status, and operational GET /health. Per the Target system selections the framework is FastAPI 0.123.10 on Python 3.10 with a layered, clean-code structure using dependency injection and strict typing. Target system is the only source of truth for implementation technologies; this document must not be used to add technologies the user did not select. Access control per route is mandatory; a wrong access level on any route would break owner isolation or role protection.
items.technical_detail: FastAPI 0.123.10, Python 3.10 (CPython), layered architecture, dependency injection, strict typing; routes: POST /api/auth/login (public), GET /api/me (authenticated), GET/POST /api/incidents (employee), GET /api/incidents/{id} (owner), PATCH /api/incidents/{id}/status (support), GET /health (operational)
source_refs: Page 6 (Section 12 backend framework selected in Target system)

functional_overview.application_objective: MiniSoporte_copy is an Android application backed by a REST API and a database that lets employees securely sign in and report internal incidents related to systems, equipment, and access. Employees track their own incidents, filter them by status, and review each incident's details and status history, while a support role advances incident statuses through a protected endpoint. The first version is deliberately small, secure, and fully buildable as an APK for internal testing.
actors: Employee (Android app user; signs in, lists, filters, creates, and views own incidents)
Support agent (backend role; updates incident status through a protected endpoint)
Operations tooling (consumes the /health endpoint and runs the development seed)
main_functionalities: Secure sign in with email and password
Sign out and local token removal
View my incidents list (newest first, only own incidents)
Filter incidents by status (All, Pending, In progress, Resolved)
Create a new incident with validated form
View incident details and status-history timeline
Support agent updates incident status (protected endpoint with history)
business_processes: An employee signs in with valid credentials and receives a signed token stored in Keystore-backed storage.
An employee reports an issue by filling a validated form; the incident is created in Pending status and appears in the list.
An employee reviews own incidents, filters them by status, and inspects details with a chronological history.
A support agent moves an incident from Pending to In progress to Resolved, and each change is recorded as an immutable history entry.
A development environment is initialized with reproducible migrations and an idempotent, secret-driven demo seed, validated via /health.
business_rules: An incident belongs to exactly one employee and employees can never view incidents owned by others.
Every new incident starts in Pending status.
Valid transitions are Pending to In progress to Resolved; a Resolved incident cannot revert in version 1.
Only the support role can update incident status.
Each status transition records previous status, new status, date, and actor; history cannot be altered by employees.
Email addresses are normalized and unique before authentication.
Failed sign-in shows a generic message that does not reveal whether the email exists.
Passwords are stored only as resistant salted hashes and never logged in plain text.
Passwords, tokens, and authorization headers are never logged; errors never expose stack traces or sensitive information.
Demo records are created only in development/demonstration, seeded idempotently from environment-supplied passwords, never automatically in production.
Data is validated on both client and server, with errors shown next to the corresponding fields.
Statuses are conveyed with text and color, never color alone, with accessible labels, contrast, and touch targets.
included_scope: Android phone app (portrait, Spanish UI, online only) for employees
REST API with authentication, incidents, owner-based authorization, and status history
PostgreSQL database with reproducible migrations for User, Incident, and IncidentHistory
Support-role status update endpoint protected by role
Unit and integration tests with 90 percent target coverage of business logic
Internal-testing debug APK build and run.apps contract
excluded_scope: Location, biometrics, Bluetooth, NFC, or microphone access
Employee editing or deletion of incidents

stack: Kotlin Android (Jetpack Compose, application id com.nexti.minisoporte, portrait, internal distribution)
patterns: Token-based session authentication with role-based authorization
Owner-based authorization on every incident query
Layered backend architecture with dependency injection and strict typing
technical_overview.code_structure: A Kotlin Android client (sign-in, incident list/filter, new incident form, details with history timeline) talking to a layered FastAPI backend backed by PostgreSQL, with pytest unit/integration tests and a build-only run.apps contract for internal distribution.
